meaning: Deeply troubled and torn apart (by guilt), as if searched roughly; usually: searched a place roughly, making a mess and stealing things

meaning: Hit or knocked quickly and sharply on a surface

meaning: Go down a steep cliff or wall by sliding down a rope fixed at the top

meaning: A friendly relationship in which people understand each other well

meaning: So interested in something that you notice nothing else

meaning: Sounding rough and harsh, like a scraping sound (of a voice or throat)

meaning: A large rodent like a big mouse; also an informal insult for a nasty or disloyal person

meaning: (... up) Increased steadily, little by little

usage.pattern: rather + adjective / would rather do something

meaning: A fixed amount of food allowed to each person or animal
trick: RATIONS = food given by RATIO.

meaning: A baby's toy that makes a noise when shaken; also a series of short knocking sounds

usage.pattern: shake a rattle / the rattle of something

meaning: Say a list of things quickly and easily, from memory
trick: RATTLE OFF = names come out fast like a RATTLE.

meaning: Nervous, worried or upset; also (... around) moved or kept going around
trick: RATTLED = shaken like a box of coins.

meaning: Making short, quick knocking sounds by shaking; also moving around inside something

meaning: Extremely beautiful

meaning: Emotionally open and exposed, with nothing hidden; also uncooked or sore

meaning: Got something as a result of what you did; also cut and gathered a crop

meaning: The act of knowing or identifying someone or something; also praise or acceptance

meaning: Activities done for enjoyment when not working

meaning: Bring food back up from the stomach; also repeat facts without understanding

Birds regurgitate food to feed their chicks.

meaning: Informal: treatment to help someone recover after injury or illness; also treatment for addiction
trick: REHAB = REHABilitation, short form.
examples: Disabled and convalescing folks head there for an afternoon's rehab stroll.
After the surgery he spent weeks in rehab.

meaning: Informal: doing exercise and treatment to recover from an injury
trick: REHABBING = doing REHAB.
examples: That summer I stayed in the Midwest, healing up then rehabbing my knee.
She is rehabbing her shoulder after the fall.

meaning: Helping someone get healthy or back to normal life after illness, injury or prison
trick: RE + HABIT → getting back into normal habits.
examples: Then, let's have you start your Rehabilitation Training, shall we?
After the surgery, he needed months of rehabilitation.

meaning: Go over or discuss something old again; also reuse old ideas with little change

Let's not rehash yesterday's argument.

meaning: The period during which someone rules or has power
trick: REIGN — the king's REIGN rains down on everyone.

The queen's reign lasted fifty years.

usage.pattern: someone's reign / during the reign of someone / reign over something

meaning: Put someone or something back into a former position or role
trick: RE-IN-STATE = put back IN the old STATE.
examples: The humans might make another attempt to recapture the farm and reinstate Mr. Jones.
The company agreed to reinstate the sacked worker.

meaning: Refusing to accept, believe or agree to something
trick: RE-JECT → throw it back (ject = throw).
examples: Rejecting the values that were instilled in you during your childhood...
He kept rejecting every idea we gave him.

meaning: Feel or show great happiness
trick: RE-JOICE = feel JOY again and again.
examples: The envious human beings would rejoice if the mill were not finished on time.
The whole town will rejoice when the team wins.

meaning: Great happiness and celebration
trick: REJOICING = everyone filled with JOY.
examples: This is a time of rejoicing and celebration.
There was great rejoicing when the baby was born.

usage.pattern: a time of rejoicing / great rejoicing

meaning: Feeling young, fresh and full of energy again
trick: RE-JUVEN-ATED = made JUVENile (young) again.
examples: Two hard miles later I felt rejuvenated.
After the holiday she came back rejuvenated.

usage.pattern: feel rejuvenated / be rejuvenated by something

meaning: To pass a message or information on to someone; also a race in teams
trick: RELAY race → pass the baton (message) on.

Please relay this message to your manager.

meaning: Agreed to something after first refusing; became less strict
trick: RELENTED = LENT (gave) in at last.

Mum finally relented and let us stay up late.

usage.pattern: someone relented / relent and do something

meaning: Never stopping or becoming weaker; very determined
trick: RELENTLESS = never RELENTs (gives in).
examples: It takes relentless self-discipline to schedule suffering into your day.
The relentless rain flooded the streets.

usage.pattern: relentless + noun / be relentless in something

meaning: An old object or custom surviving from the past
trick: RELIC = something LEFT behind (re-LICT) from long ago.
examples: The tea set was the sole relic that Nana had of her own mother.
This old coin is a relic from the British era.

meaning: Give up or let go of something, such as control, a right or a feeling
trick: RELINQUISH = RE-LINK-QUIT: quit the link, let it go.
examples: People relinquish all responsibility, demanding that society cater to their feelings.
He refused to relinquish control of the company.

meaning: Enjoy something very much; also a tasty sauce or pickle
trick: RELISH it like tasty RELISH (sauce) on your food.
examples: I didn't much relish the task and soon started smoking, staring at the sea.
She seems to relish a good challenge.

usage.pattern: relish something / relish doing something / with relish

meaning: Enjoyed something very much
trick: RELISHED like a tasty RELISH.
examples: He relished this part of the job.
The kids relished every bite of the cake.

meaning: Enjoying something very much
hindi: आनंद लेते हुए, मज़ा लेते हुए
trick: RELISHING = tasting it slowly like RELISH.
examples: She was laughing to herself, saying it over and over, relishing the words.
He was relishing his first day off in months.

meaning: A feeling of not wanting to do something
trick: RELUCTANCE = LUCK-lacking feeling: you don't want to try.
examples: There was a reluctance in her movements, and her eyes had a faraway look.
He agreed, but with obvious reluctance.

usage.pattern: reluctance to do something / with reluctance

meaning: Not wanting to do something and so slow to do it
trick: RELUCTANT = like a reluctANT ant dragging its feet.
examples: The youngest seemed reluctant to embrace his friends' air of impunity.
She was reluctant to leave the party early.

usage.pattern: be reluctant to do something / a reluctant + noun

meaning: In an unwilling, hesitant way
trick: RELUCTANTLY = doing it with dragging feet.
examples: I nodded, reluctantly, but I wasn't raised to pry into the affairs of adults.
He reluctantly agreed to clean his room.

meaning: Depend on someone or something for help or support
trick: RELY = RE-LIE: lie back on someone for support.
examples: The more you rely on them to feel better, the more you will seek them out.
You can always rely on me.

usage.pattern: rely on / upon someone / something (to do something)

meaning: Talking or thinking happily about past events
hindi: यादें ताज़ा करते हुए, अतीत याद करते हुए
trick: REMINISCING = REMINDing yourself of the past.
examples: She would always remember Babi this way: reminiscing about Mammy, elbows on the rock.
The old friends spent the evening reminiscing about school.

meaning: A small part that is left after the rest is gone
trick: REMNANT = what REMAINs.
examples: For years he lived as a bum, a discarded and forgotten remnant of society.
She made a cushion from a remnant of cloth.

meaning: A strong feeling of sadness and guilt for something wrong you did
trick: RE-MORSE = the guilt keeps tapping like MORSE code in your heart.
examples: Is he not sufficiently punished by the lifelong remorse that is to be his lot?
He showed no remorse for his lies.

usage.pattern: remorse for something / feel / show remorse

meaning: Caused someone or something to be in a certain state; also gave or provided (a service)
hindi: बना दिया, कर दिया; प्रदान किया
trick: RENDERED = turned into → the poison 'rendered' him still.
examples: Any minute now, you'll be rendered immobile by that poison.
The news rendered her speechless.

usage.pattern: render someone/something + adjective / be rendered + adjective

meaning: Causing someone or something to be in a certain state; also a performance or drawing of something
trick: RENDER — RENDERing makes something BECOME a new state.
examples: ...rendering that person unable to lie or keep secrets.
The storm cut the power, rendering the lift useless.

meaning: Acting against the rules or traditions of one's group; also a person who leaves a group
trick: RENEGADE = RENEGE (go back on a promise) — a rebel who breaks away.
examples: DEVGRU was a hard, renegade crew within the SEALs.
The renegade cop ignored his boss's orders.

meaning: Covered with a new layer of road surface
hindi: फिर से बनाई गई (सड़क), दोबारा पक्की की गई
trick: RE + PAVED = PAVED again.
examples: She hears of schools built in Kabul, roads repaved, women returning to work.
The city repaved our street last month.

usage.pattern: repave a road / road was repaved

meaning: Keeps something out or pushes it away; also, causes disgust
trick: re (back) + pel (push) = pushes back.
examples: Yet it repels moisture and won't burn easily.
This spray repels mosquitoes.

meaning: Feel and show that you are sorry for a wrong you did
trick: REPENT = RE-PAIN-T: feel the pain of your sin again.
examples: He wanted to make her repent of what she'd done.
He will repent his harsh words tomorrow.

meaning: Felt and showed sorrow for a wrong done
trick: REPENTED = said sorry after the PAIN of guilt.
examples: The mullah's son repented and said that Naghma had seduced him.
He repented and returned the stolen money.

meaning: An unexpected, usually bad result of an action
trick: REPERCUSSION = PERCUSSION (a drum hit) echoing back.
examples: I could say whatever I thought or felt, without fear of repercussion.
Skipping school had a serious repercussion for him.

meaning: Effects, usually bad, that come after an action or event
trick: RE-PERCUSSION → a drum hit echoes back again — consequences come back.
examples: It'll bring on the repercussions of forcibly switching...
Cheating in exams can have serious repercussions.

usage.pattern: repercussions of something / have repercussions for someone

meaning: All the skills, songs or acts that someone can do
trick: REPERTOIRE = a REPORT of everything you can perform.
examples: This was a new entry in his repertoire of poses: back to the wall, arms crossed.
The singer added a new song to her repertoire.

usage.pattern: someone's repertoire / a repertoire of something

meaning: Doing or saying the same thing again and again, often boring
trick: REPETITIVE = full of REPETITION.
examples: Your mind wanders when my writing becomes boring or repetitive.
Packing boxes all day is very repetitive work.

meaning: Moved and planted again in new soil or a new place
trick: RE + PLANTED = PLANTED again.
examples: Unlike weeds, I had to be replanted, you see, given food and water.
We replanted the roses in a sunny spot.

meaning: Filled with or having a lot of something
trick: REPLETE = COMPLETE-ly full (RE-PLETE, like plenty).
examples: It was a strange life, replete with fantastic, horizon-breaching experiences.
The book is replete with funny stories.

meaning: A state of rest, sleep or calm
trick: REPOSE = RE-POSE: hold a resting pose.
examples: You would not rob us of our repose, would you, comrades?
After lunch, grandfather enjoys an hour of repose.

meaning: Stop yourself from showing or feeling an emotion; also control people by force
trick: REPRESS = PRESS it back down.
examples: Many people are taught to repress their emotions, particularly negative ones.
He tried to repress a smile.

meaning: Keeping feelings hidden or controlled; also controlling people by force
trick: REPRESSION = PRESSing things back down.
examples: It leads to a life of insecurity, neuroticism, and emotional repression.
Years of repression made her afraid to cry.

meaning: A short break or relief from something bad; also cancelling a punishment
trick: REPRIEVE = RE-PRIEVE: no more GRIEVE for a while.
examples: In her hands was a welcome reprieve from more Myoplex and Ritz crackers.
The cool rain gave us a reprieve from the heat.

meaning: Spoke angrily and formally to someone for doing something wrong
trick: RE-PRI-MAND → the 'prime' boss making a 'demand' — you got scolded.
examples: Time and time again, he steadfastly reprimanded me.
The boy was reprimanded for being late.

usage.pattern: reprimand someone for (doing) something / be reprimanded

meaning: Speaking angrily and formally to someone for doing wrong
trick: REPRIMANDING = a PRIM teacher scolding you.
examples: Mariam had learned to harden herself against his ridiculing and reprimanding.
The coach was reprimanding the players for being late.

usage.pattern: reprimand someone for something / for doing something

meaning: Showing disappointment or blame for what someone did

meaning: Showed someone disappointment or blame for what they did

examples: The others reproached her sharply, and they went outside.

usage.pattern: reproach someone for something / for doing something

meaning: Showing blame or disappointment

meaning: To make someone feel strong dislike or disgust; also to drive back an attack
trick: Re (back) + pulse (push) → it pushes you back in disgust.
examples: You repulse me after all.
The smell of rotten eggs repulses me.

usage.pattern: something repulses someone / repulse an attack

meaning: Made someone feel strong dislike or disgust; also drove back an attack
hindi: घृणा पैदा की, घिनौना लगा; पीछे धकेला
trick: Re (back) + pulsed (pushed) → pushed back in disgust.
examples: The reason you repulsed me...
I was repulsed by the dirty kitchen.

usage.pattern: be repulsed by something / repulse someone

meaning: Very unpleasant; causing strong dislike
trick: RE-PULSE → pushes you back (repel) in disgust
examples: I'll exterminate those repulsive demons!
The rotten food had a repulsive smell.

usage.pattern: a repulsive + noun / find something repulsive

meaning: Needed for a particular purpose; required
trick: REQUISITE sounds like REQUIRED: what is required is requisite.
examples: If you keep chasing highs to cover the pain, you'll never find the requisite motivation to change.
She has the requisite skills for this job.

usage.pattern: the requisite + noun / requisite for something

meaning: Saved someone from danger or harm
trick: Rescue team → rescued the people.
examples: ...because he'd rescued an elderly man from bandits.
Firefighters rescued the cat from the tree.

meaning: To look like or be similar to someone or something
trick: RE-SEMBLE = SIMILAR again: re-SEMBL-e sounds like 'similar'.
examples: In fighting against Man, we must not come to resemble him.
You really resemble your father when you smile.

meaning: Felt angry and bitter about someone or something seen as unfair
trick: RE-SENT-ED: the hurt was SENT back again and again in the mind, so she resented it.
examples: I still resented my ex for what she had done.
He resented being told what to do by his younger brother.

usage.pattern: resented someone for something / resented doing something

meaning: Feeling bitter and angry about being treated unfairly
trick: RESENT-FULL: full of resentment.
examples: With each disappointment, Rasheed had grown more remote and resentful.
She felt resentful when her friends didn't invite her.

usage.pattern: be/grow resentful of someone/something / resentful about something

meaning: Soldiers who are not in full-time service but can be called up when needed
trick: RESERVE-ists: soldiers kept in RESERVE, used when needed.
examples: In BUD/S, reservists with injuries that take a long time to heal are sent home.
The army called up thousands of reservists during the war.

meaning: A large store or supply of something; also a lake used to store water
trick: RESERVoir = where something is RESERVED (kept) for later.
examples: All those tiny movements add up to a reservoir of wasted energy.
The town gets its drinking water from a reservoir in the hills.

meaning: Large stores or supplies of something; also lakes used to store water
trick: RESERVoirs = places where things are RESERVED (kept) for later.
examples: Under the hood, we all have huge reservoirs of potential.
The reservoirs are nearly empty after the dry summer.

meaning: Remaining after most of something has gone or been used
trick: RESIDUAL = RESIDUE = what is left behind.
examples: You may still find some residual dead space.
There was some residual pain after the injury healed.

meaning: To accept something bad that you cannot change (resign yourself to); also to leave a job
trick: RE-SIGN → sign off and accept your fate.
examples: You'll just have to resign yourself to fate.
He decided to resign from his job.

usage.pattern: resign yourself to something / resign from a job

meaning: Calm acceptance of something bad that cannot be changed; also leaving a job officially
trick: RE-SIGN: you SIGN off and give up, either on a job or on fighting fate.
examples: She shrugged with resignation when the bus didn't come.
He handed in his resignation on Monday.

usage.pattern: with resignation / hand in your resignation

meaning: The ability to recover quickly from difficulties
trick: RESILIENCE: like a spring that RE-SILIENTly bounces back.
examples: Teachers have noticed a lack of emotional resilience in today's young people.
Her resilience helped her get through a tough year.

usage.pattern: resilience in the face of something / show resilience

meaning: Able to recover quickly from difficulties
trick: RESILIENT ≈ RE-SLING → a rubber sling bounces back.
examples: Because of her resilient mental strength...
Children are often very resilient.

usage.pattern: be resilient (to something) / a resilient + noun

meaning: Not harmed or affected by something; also opposed to change
trick: Resist + ant → an ant that resists everything.
examples: The speed at which he becomes resistant is insane!

meaning: In a firm and determined way, without changing your mind
trick: RESOLUTE ≈ RESOLVE → firmly resolved.
examples: Resolutely indifferent.

meaning: The amount of detail or sharpness in a picture or piece of work; also a firm decision to do something

examples: The resolution on his work wasn't good enough, so he never showed it.

usage.pattern: high/low resolution / make a resolution to do something

trick: RE-SOLVE → you solve to do it again and again = strong will.
examples: It's because your resolve is too weak!

usage.pattern: someone's resolve / resolve to do something / resolve a problem

meaning: A deep feeling of connection or matching with something; also a deep, long-lasting sound
trick: RESONANCE: one SOUND (Latin sonus) echoing in another, like two hearts on the same beat.
examples: When we watch a person's face closely, our brain aligns with theirs in a process called neural resonance.
His words had a special resonance for me.

usage.pattern: have resonance for someone / resonance with something

meaning: Felt deeply connected to something; also made a deep sound that echoed
trick: RE-SONATE: the SOUND came back again inside me.
examples: He had survived the impossible, and I resonated with his survival.
Her speech resonated with everyone in the room.

meaning: Matching or vibrating together with something; also connecting with someone's feelings
trick: RE-SONA = sound again → echoing together.
examples: ...as if resonating with him.

meaning: Belonging separately to each of the people or things mentioned
trick: RESPECTIVE → each gets their own RESPECT.
examples: There'd be no reason to disperse your respective skills.

meaning: A short break from something difficult or unpleasant
trick: RESPITE: a moment to REST from SPITE.
examples: During the summers, there was no midweek respite from Trunnis.

meaning: Places where you pay to sit and eat meals
trick: RESTAURANTS: places to REST and eat.
examples: Jimmy spent as much money in bars and fine restaurants as he did on his business ideas.

usage.pattern: eat at restaurants / restaurants in/near somewhere

meaning: Restless and difficult to control, especially because unhappy
trick: RESTIVE: no REST, so they're restless and ready to rebel.
examples: The news of their defeat made the animals on nearby farms more restive than ever.

meaning: Held back from doing or showing something

meaning: Calm control over your actions or feelings

examples: Would it kill you to show some restraint?

meaning: To bring something back to life or use; also to make someone breathe again

examples: She found it exhausting to resuscitate once again what was long dead.

meaning: Kept or continued to have something
trick: RE-TAIN-ED: held (Latin tenere) on to it again.
examples: Running out of money sounded silly, but my mother retained her childhood habit.

meaning: To attack or harm someone because they attacked or harmed you

examples: ...or I won't be able to defeat them when they retaliate!

usage.pattern: retaliate against someone / retaliate for something

meaning: Attacking or harming someone in return for what they did
trick: RE-TALI-ate: Latin talio = 'eye for an eye'.
examples: The two groups kept retaliating against each other, and the fighting grew worse.

usage.pattern: retaliating against someone / retaliating for something

meaning: An action done to hurt someone because they hurt you first
trick: Re-TALI-ation: one taali for another — hit back.
examples: You were bound hand and foot out of retaliation and then burned alive.

usage.pattern: in retaliation for something / out of retaliation

trick: RETCH sounds like 'wretched': the wretched feeling before you throw up.
examples: She held the girl's hair back when she had to retch.

meaning: Made the sound and movement of vomiting

examples: Sometimes she retched again and again and threw up everything she ate.

meaning: Making the sound and movement of vomiting
trick: RETCHING: a wretched gagging sound.
examples: Each time he spat, it sounded as if he were retching.

meaning: A group of helpers or followers who go with an important person
hindi: अनुचर दल, साथ चलने वाले लोग
trick: RETINUE = RETAIN-ue: people the boss RETAINS to follow him.
examples: Napoleon was attended by his retinue of dogs.
The star arrived with a retinue of bodyguards and assistants.

meaning: A quick, sharp or clever reply; (verb) to reply in this way
trick: RE-TORT: twist (Latin torquere) the words back at someone.
examples: They heard a squeaky plea, a curt retort, and a door shut.

meaning: To take back something you said or claimed; also to pull something back in
trick: RE-TRACT: TRACTor pulls it back.
examples: I want to debate this with you and then get you to retract this theory.

meaning: A statement saying that something said earlier was wrong
trick: RETRACTION: the act of retracting = pulling back your words.
examples: The kebab man took offense and demanded a retraction.
The newspaper printed a retraction the next day.

meaning: To move back or away to a safer or quieter place
trick: RE-TREAT: go back to your room and give yourself a TREAT of peace.
examples: She would retreat back to her room and watch the snow falling.

usage.pattern: retreat to somewhere / retreat from something

meaning: Moves back or away from someone or something
trick: RE-TREATS: goes back to his corner.
examples: Apollo retreats to the opposite corner with his arms held high.

meaning: Going back to an earlier, worse state; moving backward
hindi: पिछड़ा हुआ, पीछे की ओर जाता

examples: They're just cheap imitations, retrograde versions of Sun Breathing!

meaning: Thinking about past events, often understanding them better now
hindi: पीछे मुड़कर देखना, अतीत पर नज़र

examples: One day, in retrospect, the years of struggle will strike you as the most beautiful.

meaning: Shook or echoed with a loud, repeated sound
trick: RE-VERBERATED: the VERB (word/sound) bounced back again and again.

usage.pattern: something reverberated through/around somewhere / reverberated with something

meaning: Echoing sounds that repeat as they bounce off surfaces; also long-lasting effects
trick: RE-VERB → the sound is repeated again and again.
examples: I can hear it well thanks to the reverberations.

meaning: To admire and respect someone very deeply
trick: REVERE — REVERENCE; like REVERing a guru.
examples: This is how that man treats even those who revere him!

usage.pattern: revere someone as something / be revered by someone

meaning: Deeply respected and admired
trick: REVERED: people REVERENTly bow to the revered.

usage.pattern: be revered by someone / revered as something

meaning: Showing deep and serious respect
trick: REVERENT = full of REVERENCE (deep respect), like in a temple.

usage.pattern: in a reverent manner / a reverent + noun

meaning: A pleasant state of being lost in your thoughts; a daydream
trick: REVERIE sounds like 'REVERSE': you're lost in a reverse world of dreams.
examples: At some point the reverie broke like a fever.

usage.pattern: in a reverie / break someone's reverie

meaning: Brought something back to life, strength or use
hindi: फिर से जीवित किया, पुनर्जीवित किया
trick: RE-VIVED: VIVA (life) again.
examples: Launching my ultra quest revived my stalled career.
A cup of tea revived her after the long walk.

meaning: Officially cancelled or taken away
trick: RE-VOKED: the VOICE (Latin vocare) called it back.

meaning: Felt or caused strong disgust; also rose up against authority
trick: REVOLTED: your stomach starts a REVOLT against what it sees.
examples: How could they be photographed this way? Her stomach revolted with distaste.

usage.pattern: something revolted someone / be revolted by something

meaning: A strong feeling of disgust or horror

meaning: Making an engine run faster and louder

examples: Each insult became more fuel for the engine revving inside me.

meaning: A serious medical condition in which damaged muscle breaks down and can harm the kidneys
trick: RHABDO-MYO-LYSIS: rod (rhabdo) muscle (myo) breaking (lysis).
examples: "You look like you're in rhabdomyolysis, David," she said.

meaning: A regular pattern of movement, sound or events
trick: RHYTHM Helps Your Two Hips Move.
examples: The new moon could change an entire city, alter its rhythm and mood.

usage.pattern: the rhythm of something / in rhythm

meaning: Old and weak, likely to break or fall apart
trick: RICKETY: it creaks 'rick-rick' when you touch it.
examples: It wasn't easy because of that rickety bar.
Be careful on that rickety old ladder.

meaning: A fixed, unnatural grin or open mouth, often in pain or death
trick: RICTUS sounds like RIGID + mouth: a stiff, stuck grin.
examples: His face was frozen in a rictus of fear.
She smiled a tight rictus of a smile for the camera.

usage.pattern: a rictus of + feeling / in a rictus

meaning: 'Bed-ridden' = stuck in bed through illness; '-ridden' = full of something bad; also past participle of ride
trick: Bed-RIDDEN → riding the bed all day.
examples: ...after having been bedridden for so long.
She has ridden this bike for years.

meaning: Full of holes, or full of something bad
trick: A riddle full of puzzles — riddled with holes.
examples: Look at you, riddled with needles... A comical sight, indeed!
The essay was riddled with mistakes.

meaning: A long narrow raised top of a hill or mountain
hindi: पहाड़ की चोटी की रेखा, कटक
trick: RIDGE: like the bridge of your nose, a long raised line.
examples: I was on the wrong ridge.
We walked along the ridge and saw the valley below.

meaning: The line along the top of a ridge of hills or mountains
trick: RIDGE + LINE = the line along the hilltops.
examples: The battle took place along a ridgeline above 9,000 feet.
We watched the sun set behind the ridgeline.

meaning: Unkind words or laughter that make someone look foolish
trick: RIDICULE someone and they look RIDICULOUS.
examples: Trauma can cause this, as can shame and social ridicule.
He faced ridicule for his strange haircut.

usage.pattern: face/fear ridicule / an object of ridicule

meaning: Laughed at or made to look foolish
trick: RIDICULED = made to look RIDICULOUS.
examples: She will never let on that she has had dreams that were ridiculed.
He was ridiculed for his idea, but it worked.

usage.pattern: be ridiculed for something / ridiculed someone

meaning: Laughing at someone or making them look foolish
trick: RIDICULING = making someone look RIDICULOUS.
examples: His father began ridiculing him for his laziness.
Stop ridiculing your brother's drawing.

meaning: Stiff and not able to bend; also strict and unwilling to change
trick: RIGID sounds like 'rigged': rigged so tight it won't bend.
examples: Her body tightened and became rigid during the fit.
He sat rigid in his chair, afraid to move.

meaning: A long, confusing speech or process that seems pointless
trick: RIGMAROLE: a ROLE of words that RIG-s up a long ritual.
examples: The judge began pronouncing a long rigmarole in the name of the French people.
Getting a new passport is such a rigmarole.

usage.pattern: a rigmarole of something / go through the rigmarole of doing something

meaning: Very careful, thorough and strict
trick: RIGOROUS = RIGor + OUS: full of strict rigour.
examples: Delta Selection is rigorous, and I had always been curious about it.
The new drug went through rigorous testing.

meaning: The outer edge of something round, like a wheel, cup or pot
trick: RIM: the Round Item's Margin.
examples: Mammy folded her hands on the rim of the pot.
He licked the salt off the rim of the glass.

meaning: Surrounded something in a circle
trick: RINGED: made a RING around it.
examples: The homes were the same dusty colour as the mountains that ringed the city.
Tall trees ringed the small lake.

usage.pattern: something ringed something / ringed by/with something

meaning: Washed something quickly with clean water
trick: RINSED: water RAN through it (rins-ed).
examples: She rinsed with a bowl and soaped her hair again.
He rinsed the cups before putting them away.

meaning: A long tear or cut in cloth or paper; (verb) to tear quickly
trick: RIP: the sound of cloth tearing - rrrip!
examples: Babi ran his finger through the rip.
There's a rip in the back of your jeans.

meaning: Fully grown and ready to eat (of fruit)
trick: RIPE: ready to be RIPPED from the tree.
examples: She had a chubby face like a ripe apple.
These mangoes are ripe and sweet.

meaning: Becoming fully grown and ready to eat
trick: RIPENING = becoming RIPE.
examples: The early apples were now ripening in the orchard.
The tomatoes are ripening in the sun.

meaning: Torn or pulled off quickly and violently; also, (informal) very muscular
trick: RIP → the sound of paper being torn.
examples: I ripped off her limbs, and then...
She ripped open the gift box.

meaning: Moved or spread in small waves
trick: RIPPLED: like ripples on water after a stone falls in.
examples: It rippled off my skin and poured from my soul.
The lake rippled in the breeze.

meaning: A formal ceremony or custom, often religious
trick: RITE = RITual (not 'right' or 'write').
examples: My one hope was to escape and defeat their cruel rite.
Getting your first job is a kind of rite of passage.

usage.pattern: a rite of something / perform a rite

meaning: Formal ceremonies or customs, often religious
trick: RITES = RITuals (not 'rights').
examples: She wished to be buried with the rites of the Church.
The priest performed the last rites.

usage.pattern: perform the rites / the rites of something

meaning: Fixed firmly on something, unable to look away
trick: RIVETED: fixed like a metal RIVET.
examples: His very pale, clear eyes were riveted on me.
The children were riveted to the TV screen.

usage.pattern: be riveted on/to someone/something / be riveted by something

meaning: So interesting that you cannot stop paying attention
trick: RIVETING: it RIVETS your eyes to the page.
examples: The Financial Times called the book a riveting read.
The final match was riveting from start to finish.

meaning: Cockroaches (informal)
trick: ROACHES: cock-ROACHES.
examples: I'd see roaches scurry for cover when I flipped the lights on.
The old kitchen was full of roaches.

usage.pattern: roaches scurry / get rid of roaches

meaning: To walk or travel around without a clear plan
trick: ROAM like a Roman wanders all ROAds.
examples: Millions roam the streets, addicted to comfort and unaware of their potential.
Cows roam freely on the village roads.

meaning: Did something very well (informal); also moved gently back and forth
trick: ROCKED it = performed like a ROCK star.
examples: He rocked PT and sailed through First Phase.
She totally rocked her job interview.

meaning: Moving gently backwards and forwards or from side to side
trick: ROCKING chair: moves back and forth.
examples: Next to Laila, Mammy kept rocking back and forth.
She was rocking the baby to sleep.

usage.pattern: rocking back and forth / rocking someone

meaning: Small animals with sharp front teeth, such as rats and mice
trick: RODENTS make DENTS with their teeth.
examples: I'd see dead rodents stuck to the sticky traps I had laid.
Keep food in boxes so rodents can't get in.

meaning: A show where cowboys ride wild horses and catch cattle
trick: RODEO: cowboys RODE-O horses.
examples: Back then, he was a simple Texas rodeo cowboy who barely said a word.
We watched cowboys ride bulls at the rodeo.

meaning: A long towel joined in a loop and hung on a roller, used by many people
trick: ROLLER TOWEL: a towel that ROLLS round and round on a bar.
examples: By evening the roller towel was sopping wet from being used by so many people.
There was a roller towel next to the sink in the factory.

meaning: Heavy machines with a turning cylinder used to flatten ground; also tubes for curling hair
trick: ROLLERS: things that ROLL over the field to flatten it.
examples: Electricity could run threshing machines, ploughs, rollers and reapers.
Farmers use rollers to flatten the soil after planting.

meaning: Busy and active without stopping (informal); also turning over and over
trick: ROLLING: like a ball that never stops rolling.
examples: The guy was always rolling, always on, talking about his work.
Once she starts telling stories, she keeps rolling for hours.

meaning: Thought of or described as better or more exciting than it really was
trick: ROMANTIC-ized: seen through rose-tinted ROMANTIC glasses.
examples: Many romanticized him.
People often romanticized life in the old village.

meaning: Played in a lively, noisy and happy way
trick: ROMPED: ROMP = run around like puppies.
examples: Kids romped about in new shirts and bright vests.
The puppies romped in the garden all afternoon.

meaning: A thick, strong cord made of twisted threads
trick: ROPE → tug-of-war rope
examples: I have a feeling that I shouldn't sever this rope with my Nichirin Sword.
Tie the boat with a strong rope.

usage.pattern: a rope / tie something with a rope

meaning: Strong thick cords made by twisting threads together; also (the ropes = how things work)
trick: Ropes → rope pulling, tug of war.
examples: We lit bonfires around the house and put up ropes with bells on them.
They tied the boat with ropes.

usage.pattern: tie something with ropes / learn the ropes

meaning: A string of beads used for counting prayers
trick: ROSARY: a ROSE garden of beads for prayer.
examples: Mullah Faizullah walked along the stream, twirling his rosary beads.
My grandmother prays with her rosary every morning.

meaning: Got up from bed or a seat; past of 'rise'
trick: RISE - ROSE - RISEN: the sun rose, and so did she.
examples: Nine-year-old Laila rose from bed, hungry for the sight of her friend.
He rose from his chair to greet us.

usage.pattern: rose from something / rose to your feet

meaning: A round badge made of ribbon, worn as a prize or honour
trick: ROSETTE: a ribbon shaped like a little ROSE.
examples: The warden had a Legion of Honour rosette in his buttonhole.
Our horse won a red rosette at the show.

usage.pattern: wear a rosette / win a rosette

meaning: To decay slowly and go bad
trick: ROT → rotten fruit.
examples: She's already dead, so if we leave her, she'll rot.
Fruit will rot if you leave it out too long.

usage.pattern: something rots / leave something to rot

meaning: Decayed and become weak or soft over time
trick: ROTTED: R-O-T, the rope ROTted away.
examples: Laila pictured her life as a rotted rope, snapping and unraveling.
The wooden fence had rotted in the rain.

meaning: Slowly decaying and going bad
trick: ROTTING: going ROTten.
examples: She laughed so hard that her rotting front tooth was on full display.
The smell of rotting fruit filled the kitchen.

meaning: Round and fat (polite)
trick: ROTUND = ROUND.
examples: There was a rotund old woman whose late husband was a stone carver.
The rotund shopkeeper laughed at my joke.

meaning: Red powder or cream put on the cheeks (old-fashioned word for blusher)
trick: ROUGE = French for RED.
examples: She washed it all off: tears, soapy water, rouge and mascara.
She put a little rouge on her cheeks before the party.

meaning: 'Roughed up' = hurt or beaten someone (informal)
trick: ROUGH → roughed up: treated roughly.
examples: I really got roughed up on Mt. Natagumo.
The thugs roughed him up and took his phone.

usage.pattern: rough someone up / get roughed up

meaning: Rough, noisy fighting or play (informal)
trick: ROUGH + HOUSE: rough play in the house.
examples: He told me he'd been having a roughhouse with a fellow who annoyed him.
The boys had a roughhouse in the living room and broke a lamp.

meaning: A casino game where a ball spins on a wheel and players bet on where it stops
trick: ROULETTE: French for 'little wheel' - it ROLLS.
examples: It was like putting every dollar you own on one number in roulette.
He lost all his money playing roulette.

meaning: To wake someone up; also to make someone excited or active
trick: ROUSE: a mouse could rouse a sleeping house.
examples: What if my body was so burned out that even a rescue breath couldn't rouse me?
The loud alarm didn't rouse him from sleep.

usage.pattern: rouse someone from something / rouse someone to action

meaning: Making people feel excited, eager or ready to act
trick: ROUSING speech ROUSES (wakes up) the crowd.
examples: Taraki was in the streets giving rousing speeches to demonstrators.
The coach gave a rousing talk before the final match.

meaning: A noisy argument or quarrel (British, rhymes with 'cow'); also a line of people or things (rhymes with 'go')
trick: ROW (like 'wow') = a loud WOW of shouting in a fight.
examples: One of them's the brother of that girl I had the row with.
My parents had a row about money last night.

usage.pattern: have a row with someone / a row about something

memory: press and move back and forth
meaning: To press and move your hand or something over a surface again and again
trick: RUB → rub your hands for warmth
examples: Hunch over and rub your hands together.
She rubbed her eyes when she woke up.

usage.pattern: rub something (together) / rub something on something

meaning: Things thrown away as useless; waste; also nonsense
trick: RUBBISH: RUB it off and throw it in the bin.
examples: She read scraps of newspaper which she found on the rubbish heap.
Please take the rubbish out before you go to bed.

usage.pattern: throw something in the rubbish / talk rubbish

meaning: Broken pieces of stone, brick and concrete left when a building falls or is destroyed
trick: RUBBLE = what's left after the building took a tumble (TROUBLE without a T).
examples: It was a public toilet now, nothing in it but rubble.
After the earthquake, people searched through the rubble for survivors.

usage.pattern: reduce something to rubble / in the rubble

meaning: A long march or run carrying a heavy backpack (military slang, short for rucksack); also a loose crowd
trick: RUCK = RUCKsack march.
examples: On Fridays I added a ruck run.
The soldiers finished a twelve-mile ruck before breakfast.

usage.pattern: go on a ruck / a + distance + ruck

meaning: A bag carried on the back, used by walkers and soldiers
trick: RUCKSACK = a SACK on your back (German 'Rücken' = back).
examples: We were weighed down with a fifty-pound rucksack.
He packed water and snacks into his rucksack for the hike.

meaning: Without clear direction or leadership, like a boat with no rudder
trick: A boat without a RUDDER goes nowhere: RUDDER-LESS.
examples: Avoiding rejection makes us rudderless and directionless in the long term.
After the manager left, the team felt rudderless.

meaning: (of a face) red in a healthy-looking way; also reddish
trick: RUDDY = RED-dy: rosy red cheeks.
examples: He was a pleasant-looking man, with blue eyes and ruddy cheeks.
The farmer had a ruddy face from working in the sun.

meaning: In a sudden, unpleasant way (rudely awakened); also in an impolite way
trick: Rude + ly → done in a rude way.
examples: My dormant senses have been rudely awakened and are dragging me forward.
He rudely interrupted the teacher.

meaning: Very basic and simple; not developed much
trick: RUDIMENTARY = RUDIMENTS = the first ABCs.
examples: It looked rudimentary, like something out of the hangman game we played as kids.
I have only a rudimentary knowledge of French.

meaning: A strong-smelling plant with bitter leaves and seeds, used in medicine and to ward off evil; also (verb, old-fashioned) to regret bitterly
trick: Wild RUE smoke keeps evil away; you'll RUE (regret) skipping it.
examples: She tossed a pinch of wild rue seeds into the brazier to ward off evil.
My grandmother burned rue to keep bad luck away.

meaning: Showing that you feel sorry or regretful, often with a little sad humour
trick: RUEFUL = full of RUE (regret).
examples: Laila found him standing in his study, a rueful expression on his face.
She gave a rueful smile when she saw her burnt cake.

meaning: In a way that shows sorrow or regret
trick: RUEFULLY = full of RUE, said sadly.
examples: He shook his head ruefully.
He smiled ruefully and admitted he had forgotten her birthday.

meaning: A strip of gathered or pleated cloth used as decoration on clothes; also (verb) to mess up hair or feathers
trick: A RUFFLE is a RUFFled (wavy) strip of cloth.
examples: Green cotton pants had a dotted ruffle on the cuff.
Her party dress had a pink ruffle around the hem.

meaning: (of hair, feathers or fur) made untidy or uneven; also upset or annoyed
trick: RUFFLED hair = the wind RUFFLED (shuffled) it.
examples: His hair was ruffled by the wind.
She came out of bed with ruffled hair.

usage.pattern: something is ruffled by something / ruffle someone's feathers

meaning: Moving something so that it becomes untidy or uneven, like wind in hair
trick: RUFFLING = SHUFFLING the hair about.
examples: I sit there a moment, wind ruffling my hair.
He walked past, ruffling his little brother's hair.

meaning: A thick piece of cloth covering part of a floor
trick: RUG = a small carpet you can tug.
examples: Most of us sweep our failures under the rug.
The cat likes to sleep on the rug by the fire.

usage.pattern: sweep something under the rug / on the rug

meaning: Strongly built and able to handle rough use; also rocky and wild (land); also (of a man's face) strong and attractive
trick: RUGGED = built for ROUGH roads.
examples: TV commercials want you to believe a good life means a more rugged car.
He bought a rugged phone that survives being dropped.

meaning: In a strong, rough way; '... handsome' = attractive in a strong, manly way
trick: RUGGEDLY handsome = handsome in a ROUGH, tough way.
examples: It was the face of a man with a heavy black moustache and ruggedly handsome features.
The actor was ruggedly handsome, with a strong jaw.

meaning: A long, low, deep sound, like thunder or an engine; also (verb) to make this sound
trick: RUMBLE = the deep BUMBLE of thunder.
examples: I remember the wait outside a café for the bus, and the rumble of the engine.
We heard the rumble of thunder in the distance.

usage.pattern: the rumble of something / something rumbles

meaning: Searches for something by moving things around in a careless or hurried way
hindi: टटोलता है, उलट-पलट कर खोजता है
trick: RUMMAGES = RUMMAGE sale: dig through a messy pile.
examples: Price quietly rummages through my things, checking pockets.
She rummages in her bag for her keys every morning.

meaning: A story passed from person to person that may not be true (US spelling; British 'rumour')
trick: RUMOR = ROOM-OR: the story runs from room to room.
examples: There are rumors that the socialists in Kabul helped him take power.
Don't believe every rumor you hear at the office.

usage.pattern: there is a rumor that ... / spread a rumor

meaning: To behave in a wild, uncontrolled way; to get out of control
trick: AMOK sounds like 'a muck': things run into a muck-up.
examples: Recent technology seems to allow our insecurities to run amok like never before.
The children ran amok at the party and broke a vase.

meaning: To burst or break open suddenly (especially inside the body); also a break in a relationship
trick: RUPTURE ≈ 'rapture' → so excited something bursts.
examples: Such violent moves would normally rupture his body on the spot!
The heavy rain caused the pipe to rupture.

meaning: A clever trick to fool someone
trick: RUSE = a RUSE is a RUSE-y (sneaky) trick.
examples: The trip to Ghazni had been a ruse.
The phone call was just a ruse to get him out of the house.

usage.pattern: a ruse to do something / see through a ruse

meaning: A sudden strong feeling of excitement or pleasure; also great hurry
trick: A RUSH of blood: the thrill hits you fast.
examples: That escape can provide us a quick rush that makes us feel better.
I felt a rush of joy when I saw my name on the list.

usage.pattern: a rush of + feeling / get a rush from something

meaning: Having reddish-brown hair
trick: RUSSET = RUST colour: hair the colour of rust.
examples: Sometimes he came with his russet-haired son Hamza.
The russet-haired girl sat at the front of the class.

meaning: A soft, light sound like dry leaves or paper moving; also (verb) to make this sound
trick: RUSTLE = the RUSH of leaves going 'sss'.
examples: Then came the rustle of blankets as they shifted over each other.
I heard the rustle of leaves in the garden.

meaning: Moved with a soft crackling sound, or made something do so
trick: Wind RUSTLED the trees: 'ssshh' through the leaves.
examples: A cool breeze rustled the trees and dried the sweat from my skin.
She rustled the newspaper as she turned the page.

meaning: Making a soft crackling sound, like leaves, paper or cloth moving
trick: RUSTLING skirts go 'sss' as women walk.
examples: These women were all swinging handbags and rustling skirts.
We heard a rustling sound in the bushes.

usage.pattern: rustling + leaves/skirts / a rustling in something

meaning: (of a road or path) having deep tracks made by wheels
trick: RUTTED road = wheels cut RUTS (grooves) in it.
examples: One took a rutted, uphill dirt track off the main road.
The car bumped along the rutted country lane.
